title: Opendoor Just Shut Its Entire India Office and Replaced 250 Workers With AI. Silicon Valley Is Watching.
excerpt: The real estate tech firm's exit from Chennai and Bengaluru is being called a 'watershed moment' for India's offshoring industry — and TCS's own chairman says AI agents will soon match its workforce head for head.
body:
When Opendoor CEO Kaz Nejatian posted a letter on X announcing the closure of his company's India operations, he kept it to two sentences. "Our customers are in America, and that's where our operational work belongs." Two hundred and fifty employees in Chennai and Bengaluru lost their jobs.

The move, announced on June 10, would have been unremarkable a decade ago — just another restructuring at a mid-sized proptech firm. But in 2026, the language Nejatian used — "AI-native teams," "unified systems," "smaller customer-facing teams" — landed like a manifesto. Investors and outsourcing analysts immediately seized on it as evidence of a structural shift that could redraw the map of India's $315 billion IT and outsourcing industry.

"This is not an isolated restructuring," Phil Fersht, chief executive of HFS Research, told TechCrunch. "It is part of a much broader pattern we are starting to see as companies redesign operations around AI, automation, and much leaner workflows."

Keshav Lohia, a venture capitalist at Emergent Ventures, called the decision a "watershed moment" for AI-driven operations. Sheel Mohnot, co-founder of Better Tomorrow Ventures, was blunter: "As manual work gets replaced by AI, a lot of jobs will be lost in India."

## The Numbers Behind the Anxiety

Opendoor had built its India team to handle backend workflows for its home-buying platform — the kind of manual, process-heavy work that made India the world's largest Global Capability Centre market, with more than 2,100 centres employing 2.36 million people and generating nearly $100 billion in annual revenue.

But the company's total headcount had already been shrinking. Securities filings show Opendoor employed 1,042 people globally at the end of 2025, down from 1,470 a year earlier. Its non-US workforce dropped from 342 to 184 in the same period. The India closure is the final act in a restructuring that began months ago under the banner of "Opendoor 2.0."

The real question is how many other companies are watching.

## TCS Says the Quiet Part Out Loud

The Opendoor exit landed in the same week that TCS chairman N. Chandrasekaran told shareholders that the company's employees and AI agents would soon work side by side — and that the day was "not far" when TCS would have as many AI agents as human employees. TCS employs 5.84 lakh people. It shed 23,460 jobs in the fiscal year ending March 2026.

Chandrasekaran was careful to frame AI as an opportunity, not a threat. "AI is the biggest opportunity TCS has had so far," he said. But his next line carried the edge: IT companies will hire less.

TCS had partnered with Anthropic just days earlier, equipping 50,000 workers with Claude, the AI tool whose launch in February wiped more than $62.8 billion from the market capitalisation of Indian IT firms in a single month. Infosys struck a similar deal with Anthropic in February.

Across the top six Indian IT firms, headcount fell by 71,936 in FY24 and recovered by only 15,375 in FY25. TeamLease Digital counted close to 40,000 tech layoffs in India over the past year, including mid-level managerial roles — not just freshers. The Nifty IT index has fallen 27 per cent in 2026.

## Not All Offshoring Is Equal

Analysts caution against reading Opendoor's exit as a death knell for India's entire outsourcing ecosystem. Fersht argues that the jobs being eliminated are at the base of the pyramid — process-heavy, rule-based operational roles. GCCs focused on research and development, where the work is more complex and less automatable, are still growing.

"Companies are realising that they can't save on innovation," said Jesper Ludolph, general partner at Exfinity Venture Partners. "We could potentially see GCCs working primarily on R&D expand significantly."

India's share of the MSCI Global Standard Index has shrunk from a peak of 21 per cent in September 2024 to 12.3 per cent today. But firms like Lighthouse Canton argue that India's very lack of exposure to the AI hardware trade — no chip fabs, no memory makers — could become an advantage as investors rotate out of crowded semiconductor positions in Taiwan and South Korea.

The structural shift, however, is real. AI is not just automating India's back office. It is repricing the entire cost-arbitrage model that built it.

nri_angle: For the millions of Indian IT professionals whose careers were built on the offshoring model, Opendoor's exit is a warning shot — and the restructuring of India's $315 billion IT sector will reshape job markets for NRIs and their families for years.
author: Diaspora Desk
